params.question: Why is the health planning process specifically described as a 'cycle' rather than a one-time sequence?

answers.text: Because the six phases can be rearranged in any order to suit local programme needs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The phases follow a defined order beginning with situation analysis. The term 'cycle' refers to the iterative, self-renewing nature of the process, not to flexibility of phase sequence.

answers.text: Because completing one cycle feeds evaluation data back into the next, producing continuous improvement as epidemiological realities shift

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Each cycle's monitoring and evaluation output becomes the situational input for the next cycle, creating a loop of continuous quality improvement that adapts to changing disease patterns and programme performance.

answers.text: Because the process must be completed within one calendar year before restarting from scratch

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no fixed annual timeline. The 'cycle' label reflects the iterative feedback loop — not a calendar-driven restart.

answers.text: Because planning is required only once at programme launch and is then replaced by routine administration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Health planning is never finished. The narration explicitly states it is 'perpetually renewed' — the cycle metaphor emphasises ongoing re-planning, not a one-off exercise.

overallFeedback.feedback: The planning cycle is called a 'cycle' because it is iterative — each completed cycle's evaluation data feeds back into a fresh situation analysis, enabling continuous improvement as health realities evolve.

Exactly right. The iterative nature of the planning cycle means that monitoring and evaluation data from one cycle directly informs the situation analysis of the next, creating continuous quality improvement.

interactions.label: How does Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) help a district health manager with a

params.question: How does Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) help a district health manager with a limited budget make resource allocation decisions?

answers.text: It measures patient satisfaction scores to determine which programme should receive more funding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Patient satisfaction is a separate quality metric. CEA specifically compares costs against epidemiological health outcomes such as DALYs averted, not subjective satisfaction measures.

answers.text: It converts all health outcomes into monetary values, allowing direct comparison with infrastructure costs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Converting health outcomes into monetary values is the defining feature of Cost-Benefit Analysis (CBA), not CEA. CEA deliberately keeps outcomes in natural health units.

answers.text: It eliminates the need for budget analysis by guaranteeing cost savings from every intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: CEA does not guarantee cost savings. It provides a framework for comparing relative value — which intervention yields the greatest health outcome per unit of expenditure — to inform prioritisation under budget constraints.

answers.text: It compares interventions by their cost per natural health outcome (such as cost per DALY averted), providing evidence for rational allocation among competing programme demands

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. CEA measures cost against natural health units — cost per DALY averted, cost per death prevented, or cost per case treated — allowing the manager to identify which intervention delivers the most health value per rupee spent.

overallFeedback.feedback: CEA compares the costs of interventions against natural health outcomes (e.g., cost per DALY averted or cost per death prevented), allowing a health manager to rationally allocate a limited budget to the interventions delivering the greatest health value per rupee.
Well done. CEA is the primary tool for comparing the cost of achieving a specific health outcome across different interventions, enabling evidence-based prioritisation when resources are finite.

interactions.label: The progression of India's Five-Year Plans — from the 9th Plan (health infrastru

params.question: The progression of India's Five-Year Plans — from the 9th Plan (health infrastructure expansion) to the 10th Plan (health system strengthening) to the 11th Plan (full NRHM implementation) — demonstrates which principle of health planning?

answers.text: That each plan abandoned the goals of its predecessor and started afresh with a new strategy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The plans did not abandon prior goals — they built upon them. Infrastructure expansion (9th Plan) created the base upon which system strengthening (10th) and comprehensive NRHM implementation (11th) could be layered.

answers.text: That health planning targets remained identical across all plan periods, with only the budget increasing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Targets evolved significantly — from basic infrastructure provision to system strengthening to a comprehensive national programme, reflecting accumulated learning from each planning cycle.

answers.text: That each plan built iteratively on the previous cycle's learning, evolving from basic infrastructure inputs to comprehensive system-level strengthening

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This progression illustrates the iterative planning principle in action at national scale — each plan period assessed what the previous cycle achieved, identified remaining gaps, and advanced to a more comprehensive level of health system development.

answers.text: That the Planning Commission progressively reduced its involvement in health sector allocation with each successive plan

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Planning Commission continued to allocate health sector resources until it was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015. The progression reflects deepening engagement with health system development, not withdrawal.

overallFeedback.feedback: The 9th → 10th → 11th Plan progression illustrates iterative health planning: each plan assessed what the previous cycle achieved, identified remaining gaps, and advanced from basic infrastructure provision to comprehensive NRHM implementation — a deepening, not a restart.

Exactly. The plan-wise progression from infrastructure to system strengthening to full programme implementation is a textbook example of iterative, cycle-based health planning operating at the national level.
